title: The Contrarian?: Fugue-as-Prelude and Prelude-as-Fugue No.2, Book I
content_blocks: We all know what a prelude is, right? They’re often show-off pieces for the pianist, or in their intricate and repeated use of small melodies (“motives”) they create a swirling texture that transcends the details to become something beautiful, or…or rather, we all know what, in the prelude and fugue pairing, a prelude is not, since there are so many things that it could be: it is not a highly structured piece of counterpoint, designed to show off the composer more than the pianist (or, designed to show off the pianist’s brilliant ability to play multipart counterpoint?)—for that is the role of the fugue.

Well, in my questioning of the very idea of , the approach that I took with No.2 in the first book was to switch the roles of the prelude and the fugue. What if I used something structured as the prelude, and something fast, swirling, textural and virtuosic for the fugue?

The pair begins with a gentle, mostly-chordal texture reminiscent of a Chopin Prelude (I was thinking of Op. 28 No. 4, in which almost all of the notes slowly sink inexorably downward). But this texture disguises a carefully-worked-out four-part fugue, resulting in a “Fugue-As-Prelude.” On first blush, the prelude-like quality of the fugue is clear: it begins with a minimalist accompaniment figure in the treble, followed by a simple, mostly scalar melody in the bass that climbs up about two and a half octaves before ending two octaves above the note that it started on. Melody and accompaniment—typical prelude-like texture! But as the music progresses we realize that the accompaniment is actually the first of two fugue subjects, and the melody is the second, in a four-voice double fugue. After two two-voice stretti of each subject, we have a new double-fugue section, but this time inverted (aided by the symmetrical mode—the same used for Prelude and Fugue No.4: see The Climber?, July 26, 2025), finally ending with one last presentation of the original two subjects together much as they were at the opening, sounding like a scalar melody with a minimalist accompaniment: a prelude filling the role of fugue.

Since the prelude is a fugue, and the fugue is a prelude, I think that a good name for this pair could be “The Contrarian.” Mika Sasaki’s performance is far from contrarian, though, bringing out the gentle beauty of the Fugue-as-Prelude and the swirling energy of the Prelude-as-Fugue in this combined video.
A fugue fulfills the role of a prelude, and prelude-like music forms a fugue.
